title: Lines and Angles
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Lines and Angles. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

coverage: Angle sums in triangles and polygons

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
Angle relationships

A point, line, ray and segment describe different geometric objects. Adjacent angles share a vertex and side without overlapping. A linear pair sums to 180 degrees; vertically opposite angles are equal. Perpendicular lines meet at 90 degrees.

Parallel lines

When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal, alternate interior angles are equal, and same-side interior angles sum to 180 degrees. These relationships can also establish that two lines are parallel.

Polygon angle sums

The interior-angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (\((n-2) \times 180 ^\circ\)). A regular polygon has equal interior angles, each equal to (\((n-2) \times 180/n\)) degrees. An exterior angle at each vertex sums to 360 degrees around a polygon.

Worked example: Two same-side interior angles are (\(3x+10\)) degrees and (\(2x+20\)) degrees. They sum to 180, so (\(5x+30=180\)), giving (\(x=30\)); the angles are 100 and 80 degrees.

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
• Mark the known relation on the diagram before forming an equation.
  • Distinguish equal angle pairs from supplementary pairs.
  • For a transversal, identify whether angles are corresponding, alternate or same-side before calculating.
  • Use a polygon's interior sum only after counting its sides correctly.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• Angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees; angles around a point sum to 360 degrees.
  • Vertically opposite angles are equal.
  • Triangle angle sum is 180 degrees; quadrilateral angle sum is 360 degrees.
  • For a regular n-gon, exterior angle is (\(360/n\)) degrees.

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    An angle forms a linear pair with (\(68^\circ\)). Find the angle.

    1. (\(102^\circ\))
    2. (\(112^\circ\))
    3. (\(122^\circ\))
    4. (\(292^\circ\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(112^\circ\))

    A linear pair sums to (\(180^\circ\)), so the angle is (\(180^\circ-68^\circ=112^\circ\)).

  2. Core:

    Two vertically opposite angles are formed. If one is (\(47^\circ\)), what is the other?

    1. (\(43^\circ\))
    2. (\(47^\circ\))
    3. (\(133^\circ\))
    4. (\(313^\circ\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(47^\circ\))

    Vertically opposite angles are equal, so the other angle is (\(47^\circ\)).

  3. Foundation:

    One angle in a linear pair is 68 degrees. Find the other.

    1. (\(22 ^\circ\))
    2. (\(68 ^\circ\))
    3. (\(112 ^\circ\))
    4. (\(292 ^\circ\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(112 ^\circ\))

    A linear pair sums to 180 degrees: (\(180-68=112\)) degrees.

  4. Standard:

    Parallel lines are cut by a transversal. A corresponding angle is 73 degrees. What is its alternate interior angle?

    1. (\(73 ^\circ\))
    2. (\(107 ^\circ\))
    3. (\(180 ^\circ\))
    4. (\(287 ^\circ\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(73 ^\circ\))

    Corresponding and alternate interior angles are both equal when the lines are parallel, so the angle is 73 degrees.

  5. Challenge:

    Find each interior angle of a regular decagon.

    1. (\(120 ^\circ\))
    2. (\(135 ^\circ\))
    3. (\(144 ^\circ\))
    4. (\(150 ^\circ\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(144 ^\circ\))

    The interior sum is (\((10-2) \times 180=1440\)) degrees. Divide by 10: each angle is 144 degrees.
